- Бұл **өте сирек** ауру; көбінесе **генетикалық** (мысалы, *PDHA1* гены) немес
ref: Пируватдегидрогеназа тапшылығының белгілері мен белгілері қандай? Пируватдегидрогеназа (PDH) тапшылығы ұрықтың дамуына айтарлықтай әсер етуі мүмкін, ол жүктіліктің соңында ұрықтың салмағының нашар өсуімен және жүктілік кезінде ананың зәріндегі эстриол деңгейінің төмендеуімен анықталуы мүмкін. Босану қиын болуы мүмкін және нәрестелерде Апгар баллдары төмен болуы мүмкін. Туудың төмен салмағы жиі кездеседі. PDH тапшылығымен байланысты өзіне тән қалыптан тыс көрініс бар деп болжануда, ол тар бас, көрнекті маңдай (маңдай басы), кең мұрын көпірі, ұзын филтрум және жалаңдаған танауларды қамтуы мүмкін; дегенмен, бұл барлық адамдарда байқалмайды және бұл ерекшеліктер басқа бұзылулармен бірге болуы мүмкін. Хабарланған басқа аномалияларға симиандық қыртыс, қысқа мойын, аяқ-қолдардың аздап қысқаруы, бүгу контрактуралары (бүгілген саусақтар), pes cavus (жоғары доғалы табан), сойыл табан, қарыншалық перде ақауы және гидронефроз жатады. PDH тапшылығы бар адамдар әдетте туылғаннан кейін көп ұзамай белгілерді дамытады. Жалпы, басталудың екі негізгі түрі бар: метаболикалық және неврологиялық. Метаболикалық түрі ауыр лактоацидоз түрінде көрінеді (қандағы лактаттың тым көп болуы). Бұл көбінесе емделуге жауап бермейді, осылайша мұндай ауру түрімен ауыратын көптеген адамдар жаңа туған кезеңде өледі (өте аз жағдайларда сүт ацидозы тиаминнің жоғары дозаларына жауап береді). Ауыр сүт ацидозы бар кейбір адамдарда ауыр гипераммонемия (қандағы аммиактың жоғары деңгейі) болған. Неврологиялық типті адамдарда әдетте гипотония (бұлшықет тонусының нашарлығы), нашар тамақтану және летаргия болады, кейінірек оларда құрысулар дамиды. Бұл түрі әдетте ауыр ақыл-ойдың артта қалуына, микроцефалияға (кішкентай бас), соқырлыққа және қайталама контрактуралармен (бұлшықеттер мен сіңірлердің зақымдалуы) спастикаға өтеді. Дегенмен, ұзақ мерзімді өмір сүру мүмкін және мұндай типтегі бірнеше адам жасөспірімдерге жеткен. Осы екі шектің арасында аралық формалардың үздіксіз диапазоны бар. Метаболикалық бұзылулар (лактоацидоз және гипераммонемия) ауыр емес болса, басталуы кейінірек нәрестелік кезеңге дейін кешіктірілуі мүмкін және бұл адамдарда жиі аурудан туындайтын және церебеллярлық атаксиямен (бұлшықеттің қалыптан тыс қозғалысы) байланысты сүт ацидозының үзіліссіз эпизодтары болуы мүмкін. Неврологиялық белгілері бар кейбір адамдарда Ли ауруы бар деп айтылады. PDH тапшылығы ерлер мен әйелдерде бірдей болғанымен, аурудың көрінісі олардың арасында ерекшеленеді. Метаболикалық түрі, әсіресе ауыр неонатальды лактоацидоз еркектерде әлдеқайда жиі кездеседі; созылмалы неврологиялық түрі әйелдерде жиі кездеседі. Адам фенотипінің онтологиясы пируватдегидрогеназа тапшылығының келесі белгілері мен симптомдарының тізімін береді. Егер ақпарат бар болса, төмендегі кестеде осы аурумен ауыратын адамдарда симптомның қаншалықты жиі кездесетіні көрсетілген. q: Пируватдегидрогеназа тапшылығының белгілері қандай?

answer:
**Лихен планусының пигментті нұсқасы** — бұл классикалық лихен планусының кері қалдығы немесе аралас нұсқасы. Оны анықтау үшін мынадай белгілерге көңіл аудару керек:

**Клиникалық белгілер:**
- Аурудың орналасуы: көбінесе **алдыңғы қабаттық** (ішкі арқа, қолтық асты, жамбас) және **ауыз бас аймағы** (қоңырау тәрізді, көбіне екі жақты).
- Түсі: **қоңыр-қоңыр, күңгірт-қызғылт, кейде қара** түсті, шырының қалдығына ауысатын **полосалар** немесе **дақтар**.
- Поверхностасы: кейде **тегіс, жылтыр**, кейде **түйнек** қалдықтары (темекі тәрізді) байқалады.
- Сипаты: **иттерланбайды**, бірақ **керіктеу** (темірлену) сезімдері болуы мүмкін.

**Айырудағы негізгі белгілер:**

Адам фенотипінің онтологиясы қысқа бойлық синдромы, Брюссель типіндегі белгілер мен симптомдардың келесі тізімін береді. Егер ақпарат бар болса, төмендегі кестеде осы аурумен ауыратын адамдарда симптомның қаншалықты жиі кездесетіні көрсетілген. Осы медициналық терминдердің анықтамаларын іздеу үшін MedlinePlus медициналық сөздігін пайдалануға болады. Белгілері мен симптомдары Науқастардың шамамен саны (болған кезде) Метаболизм/гомеостаз бұзылысы - Эпифиз сүйектенуінің кешігуі - Жылқының бүйрегі - Микроретрогнатия - Тар кеуде - Салыстырмалы макроцефалия - Бойдың қысқа болуы - Үшбұрышты бет - Адамның фенотипі Онтологияның белгілері немесе жиі пайда болғаны туралы ақпарат (НПО-да) шарт. Бұл ақпараттың көп бөлігі Orphanet, сирек кездесетін аурулардың еуропалық дерекқорынан алынған. Белгінің немесе симптомның жиілігі әдетте осы қасиетке ие емделушілердің пайызын шамамен бағалау ретінде тізімделеді. Жиілікті бөлшек ретінде де көрсетуге болады. Бөлшектің бірінші саны - бұл симптом қанша адамда болғаны, ал екінші сан - бір зерттеуде тексерілген адамдардың жалпы саны. Мысалы, 25/25 жиілігі 25 адамға жүргізілген зерттеуде барлық пациенттерде бұл симптомның бар екені анықталды. Бұл жиіліктер белгілі бір зерттеуге негізделгендіктен, пациенттердің басқа тобы зерттелсе, фракциялар әртүрлі болуы мүмкін. Кейде жиілік туралы ақпарат жоқ. Мұндай жағдайларда белгі немесе симптом сирек немесе жалпы болуы мүмкін.

Неonatalды доминантты отбасылық конвульсия (autosomal dominant neonatal epilepsy, ADNE) — **KCNQ2** немесе **KCNQ2/3** гендеріндегі патологиялардың нәтижесінде пайда болатын сирек кездесетін отбасылық эпилепсиялық синдром. Оның негізгі белгілері:

**1. Жасы мен басталу**
- Суда тұқымдайтын судаған балалардың көпшілігінде суда тұқымдамалар бірінші күндерден бастапты (әдетте 24–78 сағат ішінде) байқалады.
- Суда тұқымдамалар әдетте 1–3 минутқа созылады.

- Суда тұқымдамалар кезінде дененің қатуы, кейде «жабық» суда тұқымдау байқалады.
- Суда тұқымдамалардың көпшілігі генетикалық түрде анықталады.

**3. ЭЭМ-де суда тұұлдырылу**
- Суда тұқымдамалардың классикалық ЭЭМ-де **«колючий рис»** («spiky rice») пішінімен сипатталады.

- **Анықтамаға қабылдау:** қан және сүтке арналған сынақтар (толық қан саны, эозинофильдердің саны, аллергиялық маркерлер, ішектен аурудың өзгеше белгілерін тексеру)
- **Кей жағдайда:** ішектің арнаулы зерттеулері (мисалы, эндоскопия арқылы қабық қабатыын алушы) немесе гистологиялық зерттеу
- **Дифференциалдық диагностика:** басқа тереңді ішектен ауруларды (мисалы, қабыну, аллергия, инфекция) ескере отырып, анықтау

**Ескеру:** Бұл тек жалпы ақпарат. Егер сізде ұзаққа созылатын ішектен ауру, құсу, іш сұмсамақ, немесе қанық эозинофильдің артуы сияқты белгіл

Эндоскопия кезінде гастроэнтеролог эндоскоп арқылы асқазан-ішек жолдарын қарайды және патолог дәрігер қарайтын бірнеше шағын үлгілерді (биопсия) алады. Эозинофилдердің жоғары саны эозинофильді энтеропатия диагнозын болжайды. Патолог сонымен қатар эозинофилдердің орналасуын, тіндік қабаттардағы өзгерістерді және дегрануляцияны (эозинофилдердің мазмұнын төгу) қарайды. Эозинофилдер әдетте өңештен басқа асқазан-ішек жолдарының барлық аймақтарында аз мөлшерде болуы мүмкін. Дегенмен, эозинофильді энтеропатиясы бар адамдарда байқалатын эозинофилдердің саны әлдеқайда жоғары. Эозинофилді энтеропатия диагнозы расталғаннан кейін, әдетте емдеуді бағыттау үшін тағамдық аллергия сынағы ұсынылады. q: Өт қабының қатерлі ісігінің белгілері қандай?

answer:
«Лейкоэнцефалопатия» — бұл мидың ақ қабығының (миелиннің) зақымдануынан пайда болатын жалпы атау. Олардың арасында «акQUIRED» (жүктілік) және «неакQUIRED» (жүктілік емес) түрлері бар.

**Жүктілік (акQUIRED) лейкоэнцефалопатия** — бұл дүниежүзінде әртүрлі жиіліктерде кездеседі. Мысалы, құбылыстың ең таралған түрі — **спорадикалық акQUIRED иммунды лейкоэнцефалопатия (АЛ)**, ол сирек кездеседі: шамамен **100 000-нан 1 миллионға дейін** адамнан бір. Басқа түрлері (мысалы, жүктілікке байланысты немесе наследственость бойынша)әлі де сирек кездеседі.

Ең маңыздысы — аурудың белгілері мен өзгерістері бар адамдарға кешенді бағдарлама керек дегенін ескеру. Егер сізде немесе жақын адамда бұлай нәрсе болса, дәрігерге жүгіну қажет.

Егер аурудың белгілерімен қатар еңбек әлеуеті, есту, көру немесе көру бұзылыстары бар адамдардың саны туралы дерек
ref: Ақ заттың жоғалуы бар лейкоэнцефалопатияның таралуы белгісіз. Бұл сирек кездесетін ауру болса да, бұл ақ затқа әсер ететін ең көп таралған тұқым қуалайтын аурулардың бірі болып саналады.
q: Қанша адам ақ заттың жоғалуы бар лейкоэнцефалопатиямен ауырады?

Пируватдегидрогеназа (PDH) тапшылығы әдетте дене жасушаларында маңызды химиялық реакция үшін қажет бір немесе бірнеше ферменттердің немесе кофакторлардың (тиамин сияқты) жетіспеушілігінен туындайды. Бұл ферменттер немесе кофакторлар пируватдегидрогеназа кешенінің бөлігі болып табылады және әдетте пируват деп аталатын химиялық затты ацетил-коэнзим А (КоА) деп аталатын басқа химиялық затқа айналдырады (немесе түрлендіруге көмектеседі), бұл организм жасушалар үшін цитрат жасау үшін қажет екі маңызды химиялық заттардың бірі. Пируваттың ацетил-КоА-ға айналуы мүмкін емес болғандықтан, жасушаларда пируват тым көп, содан кейін ол көбірек сүт қышқылын (көп мөлшерде улы) және аланин шығаруға үйренеді; Сондай-ақ организмде цитрат жеткіліксіз. Цитрат - бұл лимон қышқылының циклі деп аталатын химиялық реакциялардың басқа маңызды тобының алғашқы қадамы, содан кейін ол жалғаса алмайды. Дене ацетил-КоА-ны көбірек өндіру үшін балама жолдар жасауға тырысады, бірақ денеде, әсіресе орталық жүйке жүйесінде (ОЖЖ) өндірілген энергия әлі де жеткіліксіз. Жетіспейтін энергия мөлшері жетіспейтін ферменттің мөлшеріне байланысты. Бұл жағдайды кейде пируватдегидрогеназа кешені (PDHC) тапшылығы деп атайды, себебі реакцияда әдетте қолданылатын үш ферменттің «кешені» бар; Жоғарыда сипатталған реакцияға қажетті ферменттердің кез келгені немесе бірнешеуі жетіспесе, жағдай нәтиже береді. Пируватдегидрогеназа тапшылығының ең көп тараған түрі Х-байланысты доминантты E1 альфа генінің мутацияларынан туындайды; барлық басқа себептер рецессивті гендердің мутацияларына байланысты деп есептеледі.

Адамдың қол-аяғының, қол-аяғының зақымданбағаны да, күш жеткілікті де, ал көрікінен және естуінен де жақсы, бірақ ол **қажын қимылды орындауға қабілетті**, мысалы, қағазды кесуге, су құюғя, көзілді-өлшегішті пайдалануға қабілетті.

Кез-келген кез-келген адамда кездесе береді, бірақ жиі неврологиялық ауруларда (мишалы, инсульт, деменция, Паркинсон ауруы) байқалады.

Егер сізде немесе жақындарыңызда осылай белгілер байқалса, **ми зақымдалуы немесе қозғалыс жүйесінің ауруы** болуы мүмкін, сондықтан дереу дәрігерге көріну керек.
ref: Апраксия (жеңіл болса, «диспраксия» деп аталады) - бұл қалауы мен физикалық қабілетіне қарамастан, білікті қозғалыстар мен ым-ишараларды орындау немесе орындау қабілетінің жоғалуымен сипатталатын неврологиялық ауру. Апраксия мидың ми жарты шарларының, әсіресе париетальды лобтың дисфункциясы нәтижесінде пайда болады және көптеген аурулардан немесе мидың зақымдануынан туындауы мүмкін.  Апраксияның бірнеше түрі бар, олар жеке немесе бірге пайда болуы мүмкін. Ең жиі кездесетіні - бет-жақ немесе ауыз-бет апраксиясы, ол ерін жалау, ысқыру, жөтелу немесе көзді қысу сияқты команда бойынша бет қимылдарын орындау мүмкін еместігін тудырады. Апраксияның басқа түрлеріне аяқ-кинетикалық апраксия (қолмен немесе аяқпен ұсақ, дәл қозғалыстар жасай алмау), идеомоторлы апраксия (ауызша бұйрыққа жауап ретінде дұрыс қозғалыс жасай алмау), идеялық апраксия (киіну, жуыну және шомылу сияқты бірнеше ретті қозғалыстармен әрекеттерді үйлестіре алмау) жатады. ауыз және сөйлеу қимылдары), конструкциялық апраксия (қарапайым фигураларды көшіру, сызу немесе құрастыру қабілетсіздігі) және окуломоторлы апраксия (бұйрық бойынша көзді жылжыту қиындығы). Апраксия афазия деп аталатын тілдің бұзылуымен бірге жүруі мүмкін. Кортикобазальды ганглионды дегенерация - бұл апраксияның әртүрлі түрлерін тудыратын ауру, әсіресе егде жастағы адамдарда.

answer: Weaver syndrome is a condition that affects many parts of the body, including the skeleton and heart. People with this disorder have unusually long limbs and fingers (polydactyly), which can be caused by extra bones in the hands and feet. They also have distinctive facial features such as a prominent forehead, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), a broad nose, and a small chin. Other signs and symptoms of Weaver syndrome include an enlarged heart (cardiomegaly) and abnormal development of the brain's blood vessels (cerebral vasculopathy). Affected individuals may also have intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe. The severity of the condition varies among affected individuals; some people with Weaver syndrome have only minor skeletal abnormalities while others have more serious health problems. Most cases of Weaver syndrome result from new mutations in the EZH2 gene and occur in people with no history of the disorder in their family. A few families with multiple members having Weaver syndrome have been reported. In these cases, the condition appears to have been inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
ref: Weaver syndrome is a rare condition that is characterized primarily by tall stature. Other signs and symptoms of the condition may include macrocephaly (unusually large head size); intellectual disability; distinctive facial features; camptodactyly (permanently bent digits) of the fingers and/or toes; poor coordination; soft and doughy skin; umbilical hernia; abnormal muscle tone; and a hoarse, low-pitched cry during infancy. Some studies also suggest that people affected by Weaver syndrome may have an increased risk of developing neuroblastoma. Weaver syndrome is usually caused by changes (mutations) in the EZH2 gene. Although the condition is considered autosomal dominant, most cases occur as de novo mutations in people with no family history of the condition. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.

answer: There is no vaccine available to protect against AHF, and there is no known way to prevent infection by the virus. However, people who live in areas where AHF has been reported should avoid contact with animals that may be infected with the virus. People who travel to these areas should also take precautions to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes. These include: Wearing long-sleeved shirts and pants when outdoors; Using insect repellent on exposed skin and clothing; Sleeping under mosquito nets if staying in an area where mosquitoes are active at night.
ref: Given that no treatment or specific prophylaxis is presently available, prevention and increased awareness of AHFV are the only recommended measures. Complete control of ticks and interruption of the virus life cycle is impractical; in endemic regions, it is important to avoid tick-infested areas and to limit contact with livestock and domestic animals. Individuals should use tick repellants on skin and clothes and check skin for attached ticks, removing them as soon as possible. Tick collars are available for domestic animals, and dipping in acaricides is effective in killing ticks on livestock. People working with animals or animal products in farms or slaughterhouses should avoid unprotected contact with the blood, fluids, or tissues of any potentially infected or viremic animals.

answer: The most common complication of HUS is acute kidney failure, which can be life-threatening. Acute kidney failure occurs when the kidneys stop working properly and cannot filter waste products from the blood. The kidneys may recover their normal function within 2 to 3 weeks after recovery from HUS. However, some children who have had HUS will continue to have chronic kidney disease (CKD) into adulthood. CKD is defined as kidney damage that lasts at least three months and causes a reduced ability to remove wastes and extra fluid from the body. In addition, some children who have had HUS develop high blood pressure, anemia, and/or low platelet counts. Anemia is a condition in which the number of red blood cells is lower than normal. Low platelet counts increase the risk of bleeding.
ref: Most children who develop hemolytic uremic syndrome and its complications recover without permanent damage to their health.1 However, children with hemolytic uremic syndrome may have serious and sometimes life-threatening complications, including - acute kidney injury - high blood pressure - blood-clotting problems that can lead to bleeding - seizures - heart problems - chronic, or long lasting, kidney disease - stroke - coma
q: What are the complications of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome in Children?

answer: There is no cure for GBS, but there are several ways to treat it. The first step is to stop any medication that may be causing the condition. If you have an infection, your doctor will prescribe antibiotics or antiviral drugs. Your doctor also may recommend intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy. This treatment involves giving you high doses of antibodies from healthy donors through an IV. It can help reduce inflammation and speed up recovery. Another treatment option is plasmapheresis. This procedure removes harmful antibodies from your blood. Plasmapheresis usually is done in a hospital by a health care provider who specializes in treating people with neurological disorders. You'll need to stay in the hospital during this treatment. Afterward, you may need to take medications to prevent infections. Physical therapy and occupational therapy also can help you recover. These therapies can help you regain strength and coordination.
ref: There is no known cure for Guillain-Barr syndrome, but therapies can lessen the severity of the illness and accelerate the recovery in most patients. There are also a number of ways to treat the complications of the disease. Currently, plasmapheresis (also known as plasma exchange) and high-dose immunoglobulin therapy are used. Plasmapheresis seems to reduce the severity and duration of the Guillain-Barr episode. In high-dose immunoglobulin therapy, doctors give intravenous injections of the proteins that in small quantities, the immune system uses naturally to attack invading organism. Investigators have found that giving high doses of these immunoglobulins, derived from a pool of thousands of normal donors, to Guillain-Barr patients can lessen the immune attack on the nervous system. The most critical part of the treatment for this syndrome consists of keeping the patient's body functioning during recovery of the nervous system. This can sometimes require placing the patient on a ventilator, a heart monitor, or other machines that assist body function.
q: What are the treatments for Guillain-Barr Syndrome?

answer: Wagner syndrome is an inherited condition that affects the development of many parts of the body, particularly the eyes and ears. People with this disorder have small, round eyes (microphthalmia) and a lack of tissue between the eyelids (ectopic palpebral fissure). They also have hearing loss due to abnormalities of the inner ear (sensorineural hearing loss). Other features may include heart defects, kidney problems, and malformations of the bones of the hands and feet. The signs and symptoms of Wagner syndrome vary widely among affected individuals. This condition is caused by mutations in the PAX6 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
ref: Wagner syndrome is a hereditary disorder that causes progressive vision loss. The eye problems that lead to vision loss typically begin in childhood, although the vision impairment might not be immediately apparent. In people with Wagner syndrome, the light-sensitive tissue that lines the back of the eye (the retina) becomes thin and may separate from the back of the eye (retinal detachment). The blood vessels within the retina (known as the choroid) may also be abnormal. The retina and the choroid progressively break down (degenerate). Some people with Wagner syndrome have blurred vision because of ectopic fovea, an abnormality in which the part of the retina responsible for sharp central vision is out of place. Additionally, the thick, clear gel that fills the eyeball (the vitreous) becomes watery and thin. People with Wagner syndrome develop a clouding of the lens of the eye (cataract). Affected individuals may also experience nearsightedness (myopia), progressive night blindness, or a narrowing of their field of vision. Vision impairment in people with Wagner syndrome can vary from near normal vision to complete loss of vision in both eyes.
q: What is Wagner syndrome?

answer: Mutations in the EPOX gene cause eosinophil peroxidase deficiency. The EPOX gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called eosinophil peroxidase, which is found in white blood cells called eosinophils. These cells play a role in immune responses by attacking foreign invaders such as bacteria and viruses. In addition, eosinophils help regulate inflammation, which is the body's response to injury or infection. Eosinophil peroxidase is involved in several steps of the inflammatory process. It helps protect eosinophils from self-destruction (apoptosis) by removing toxic molecules that would otherwise damage these cells. This enzyme also plays a role in the release of other proteins that are important for immune function. Mutations in the EPOX gene lead to the production of an abnormal version of eosinophil peroxidase. As a result, this enzyme cannot perform its normal functions. A lack of functional eosinophil peroxidase impairs the ability of eosinophils to fight infections and control inflammation. However, it is unclear how the absence of this enzyme leads to the specific signs and symptoms of eosinophil peroxidase deficiency.
ref: Mutations in the EPX gene cause eosinophil peroxidase deficiency. The EPX gene provides instructions for making the eosinophil peroxidase protein. During an immune response, activated eosinophils release eosinophil peroxidase at the site of injury. This protein helps form molecules that are highly toxic to bacteria and parasites. These toxic molecules also play a role in regulating inflammation by fighting microbial invaders. EPX gene mutations reduce or prevent eosinophil peroxidase production or result in a protein that is unstable and nonfunctional. As a result, eosinophils have severely reduced amounts of eosinophil peroxidase or none at all. Other proteins within affected eosinophils are normal, and while the cells lacking eosinophil peroxidase are smaller and may have structural changes, the loss of eosinophil peroxidase does not appear to impair the function of eosinophils.
q: What are the genetic changes related to eosinophil peroxidase deficiency?

answer: Donohue syndrome is caused by mutations in the POMGNT1 gene. This gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 1 (PNAGAT). PNAGAT is involved in the production of a sugar molecule called sialic acid, which is found on the surface of cells and plays important roles in cell signaling and communication. Sialic acid is also involved in the breakdown of certain proteins that are no longer needed. Mutations in the POMGNT1 gene lead to the production of an abnormally short version of PNAGAT. The shortened protein is not functional, so it cannot help produce sialic acid. As a result, there is a shortage of this sugar molecule. It is unclear how a lack of sialic acid leads to the specific features of Donohue syndrome. Researchers suspect that the shortage of sialic acid may affect the development of many different tissues and organs during early embryonic development.
ref: Donohue syndrome results from mutations in the INSR gene. This gene provides instructions for making a protein called an insulin receptor, which is found in many types of cells. Insulin receptors are embedded in the outer membrane surrounding the cell, where they attach (bind) to insulin circulating in the bloodstream. This binding triggers signaling pathways that influence many cell functions. The INSR gene mutations that cause Donohue syndrome greatly reduce the number of insulin receptors that reach the cell membrane or disrupt the function of these receptors. Although insulin is present in the bloodstream, without functional receptors it cannot exert its effects on cells and tissues. This severe resistance to the effects of insulin impairs blood sugar regulation and affects many aspects of development in people with Donohue syndrome.
q: What are the genetic changes related to Donohue syndrome?

answer: Arrhythmias can affect people of all ages, but they are more common as you get older. The risk increases if you have other heart problems such as coronary heart disease (CHD), heart failure, or an abnormal heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. You also may be at higher risk if you: Have certain genetic conditions that cause arrhythmias. For example, long QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome are inherited disorders that can lead to dangerous arrhythmias. Take medicines that can trigger arrhythmias. These include some antidepressants, antihistamines, decongestants, and asthma medications. Have had a heart attack. A heart attack can damage the heart muscle and disrupt its electrical system. This can lead to arrhythmias. Have a history of sudden cardiac death. Sudden cardiac death is when someone dies suddenly from a heart problem. It often happens during physical activity. If you've had sudden cardiac death, your doctor may recommend that you wear a device called an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD). An ICD detects dangerous arrhythmias and delivers shocks to restore normal heart rhythm.
ref: Arrhythmias are very common in older adults. Atrial fibrillation (a common type of arrhythmia that can cause problems) affects millions of people, and the number is rising. Most serious arrhythmias affect people older than 60. This is because older adults are more likely to have heart disease and other health problems that can lead to arrhythmias. Older adults also tend to be more sensitive to the side effects of medicines, some of which can cause arrhythmias. Some medicines used to treat arrhythmias can even cause arrhythmias as a side effect. Some types of arrhythmia happen more often in children and young adults. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), including Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, is more common in young people. PSVT is a fast heart rate that begins and ends suddenly. Major Risk Factors Arrhythmias are more common in people who have diseases or conditions that weaken the heart, such as: Heart attack Heart failure or cardiomyopathy, which weakens the heart and changes the way electrical signals move through the heart Heart tissue that's too thick or stiff or that hasn't formed normally Leaking or narrowed heart valves, which make the heart work too hard and can lead to heart failure Congenital heart defects (defects present at birth) that affect the heart's structure or function Other conditions also can raise the risk for arrhythmias, such as: High blood pressure Infections that damage the heart muscle or the sac around the heart Diabetes, which increases the risk of high blood pressure and coronary heart disease Sleep apnea, which can stress the heart because the heart doesn't get enough oxygen An overactive or underactive thyroid gland (too much or too little thyroid hormone in the body) Several other risk factors also can raise your risk for arrhythmias. Examples include heart surgery, certain drugs (such as cocaine or amphetamines), or an imbalance of chemicals or other substances (such as potassium) in the bloodstream.
q: Who is at risk for Arrhythmia??

answer: Hematuria means blood in your urine. It can be caused by - Kidney stones - Infections - Cancers of the kidney, bladder, ureter, or prostate - Trauma to the urinary tract - Certain medicines - Blood disorders - Other conditions such as lupus and multiple myeloma If you have hematuria, it may not cause any symptoms other than blood in your urine. Sometimes, however, you may feel pain when urinating. You may also notice that your urine looks pink, red, or brown. Your doctor will diagnose the cause of your hematuria based on your medical history, physical exam, and tests. Treatment depends on what's causing the bleeding. answer: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a lung disease that affects premature babies. It causes the lungs to be underdeveloped and inflamed. The inflammation can damage the air sacs, called alveoli, which are needed for breathing. BPD usually occurs in babies who were born before 37 weeks of pregnancy. These babies have underdeveloped lungs and need extra oxygen after birth. They also may have other health problems such as - Heart defects - Gastroesophageal reflux - Seizures - Neurological disorders - Blood disorders - Infections If your baby has BPD, he or she will need special care at a hospital. He or she may need oxygen therapy, which delivers oxygen through a mask or tube. Some babies also need mechanical ventilation, which uses machines to help them breathe. Most babies with BPD grow out of it by age 18 months. However, some children continue to have breathing problems into adulthood. NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
ref: Bronchopulmonary (BRONG-ko-PUL-mo-NAR-e) dysplasia (dis-PLA-ze-ah), or BPD, is a serious lung condition that affects infants. BPD mostly affects premature infants who need oxygen therapy (oxygen given through nasal prongs, a mask, or a breathing tube). Most infants who develop BPD are born more than 10 weeks before their due dates, weigh less than 2 pounds (about 1,000 grams) at birth, and have breathing problems. Infections that occur before or shortly after birth also can contribute to BPD. Some infants who have BPD may need long-term breathing support from nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) machines or ventilators. Overview Many babies who develop BPD are born with serious respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). RDS is a breathing disorder that mostly affects premature newborns. These infants' lungs aren't fully formed or aren't able to make enough surfactant (sur-FAK-tant). Surfactant is a liquid that coats the inside of the lungs. It helps keep them open so an infant can breathe in air once he or she is born. Without surfactant, the lungs collapse, and the infant has to work hard to breathe. He or she might not be able to breathe in enough oxygen to support the body's organs. Without proper treatment, the lack of oxygen may damage the infant's brain and other organs. Babies who have RDS are treated with surfactant replacement therapy. They also may need oxygen therapy. Shortly after birth, some babies who have RDS also are treated with NCPAP or ventilators (machines that support breathing). Often, the symptoms of RDS start to improve slowly after about a week. However, some babies get worse and need more oxygen or breathing support from NCPAP or a ventilator. If premature infants still require oxygen therapy by the time they reach their original due dates, they're diagnosed with BPD. Outlook Advances in care now make it possible for more premature infants to survive. However, these infants are at high risk for BPD. Most babies who have BPD get better in time, but they may need treatment for months or even years. They may continue to have lung problems throughout childhood and even into adulthood. There's some concern about whether people who had BPD as babies can ever have normal lung function. As children who have BPD grow, their parents can help reduce the risk of BPD complications. Parents can encourage healthy eating habits and good nutrition. They also can avoid cigarette smoke and other lung irritants.
q: What is Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia?

answer: Summary : A cold is caused by many different viruses. It can make you sneeze, cough, run your nose, and feel achy. You may also get a sore throat. The symptoms usually last 7 to 10 days. There's no cure for the common cold. But there are ways to treat its symptoms. Over-the-counter medicines can help relieve some of them. They include - Decongestants - Antihistamines - Pain relievers - Cough suppressants - Throat lozenges Some people use these medicines to treat their colds. Others take them to prevent colds. However, taking these medicines without talking to your doctor could be dangerous. For example, decongestants shouldn't be taken by people who have high blood pressure. Also, antihistamines should not be used by children younger than 2 years old. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
ref: Summary : Sneezing, sore throat, a stuffy nose, coughing -- everyone knows the symptoms of the common cold. It is probably the most common illness. In the course of a year, people in the United States suffer 1 billion colds. What can you do for your cold or cough symptoms? Besides drinking plenty of fluids and getting plenty of rest, you may want to take medicines. There are lots of different cold and cough medicines, and they do different things. - Nasal decongestants - unclog a stuffy nose - Cough suppressants - quiet a cough - Expectorants - loosen mucus so you can cough it up - Antihistamines - stop runny noses and sneezing - Pain relievers - ease fever, headaches, and minor aches and pains Here are some other things to keep in mind about cold and cough medicines. Read labels, because many cold and cough medicines contain the same active ingredients. Taking too much of certain pain relievers can lead to serious injury. Do not give cough medicines to children under four, and don't give aspirin to children. Finally, antibiotics won't help a cold. Food and Drug Administration

answer: Your endocrine system makes hormones, which are chemicals that control your body's many functions. The glands of the endocrine system include - The pituitary gland, located at the base of the brain - The thyroid gland, located in the neck below the Adam's apple - The parathyroid glands, four small glands on each side of the thyroid - The adrenal glands, two glands above each kidney - The pancreas, an organ behind the stomach and in front of the spine - The gonads, the testes in men and ovaries in women Your endocrine system helps regulate your metabolism, growth, mood, and sexual function. It also controls how much energy you have, how fast you burn it, and how your muscles and bones grow. Problems with the endocrine system can cause diseases such as diabetes, hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, and Cushing syndrome. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
ref: Your endocrine system includes eight major glands throughout your body. These glands make hormones. Hormones are chemical messengers. They travel through your bloodstream to tissues or organs. Hormones work slowly and affect body processes from head to toe. These include - Growth and development - Metabolism - digestion, elimination, breathing, blood circulation and maintaining body temperature - Sexual function - Reproduction - Mood If your hormone levels are too high or too low, you may have a hormone disorder. Hormone diseases also occur if your body does not respond to hormones the way it is supposed to. Stress, infection and changes in your blood's fluid and electrolyte balance can also influence hormone levels. In the United States, the most common endocrine disease is diabetes. There are many others. They are usually treated by controlling how much hormone your body makes. Hormone supplements can help if the problem is too little of a hormone.
q: What is Endocrine Diseases?

answer: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) deficiency is an inherited condition that affects the body's ability to regulate many important functions, including appetite and weight control, skin pigmentation, and sexual development. People with POMC deficiency have severe obesity from birth because they cannot sense when they are full. They also have abnormally darkened skin (hyperpigmentation), which can be noticeable at birth but usually becomes less obvious as the affected person ages. In addition, people with this disorder may have delayed puberty and reduced sex hormone levels. The signs and symptoms of POMC deficiency vary among affected individuals. Some people with POMC deficiency do not have any of these features.
ref: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) deficiency causes severe obesity that begins at an early age. In addition to obesity, people with this condition have low levels of a hormone known as adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and tend to have red hair and pale skin. Affected infants are usually a normal weight at birth, but they are constantly hungry, which leads to excessive feeding (hyperphagia). The babies continuously gain weight and are severely obese by age 1. Affected individuals experience excessive hunger and remain obese for life. It is unclear if these individuals are prone to weight-related conditions like cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes. Low levels of ACTH lead to a condition called adrenal insufficiency, which occurs when the pair of small glands on top of the kidneys (the adrenal glands) do not produce enough hormones. Adrenal insufficiency often results in periods of severely low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) in people with POMC deficiency, which can cause seizures, elevated levels of a toxic substance called bilirubin in the blood (hyperbilirubinemia), and a reduced ability to produce and release a digestive fluid called bile (cholestasis). Without early treatment, adrenal insufficiency can be fatal. Pale skin that easily burns when exposed to the sun and red hair are common in POMC deficiency, although not everyone with the condition has these characteristics.
q: What is proopiomelanocortin deficiency?

answer: Potocki-Lupski syndrome (PLS) is an inherited condition that affects many parts of the body, including the brain and nervous system, heart, bones, and genitalia. The signs and symptoms vary widely among affected individuals. Most people with PLS have developmental delay and intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe. They may also experience seizures, behavioral problems, and/or autism spectrum disorder. Other features can include distinctive facial characteristics; skeletal abnormalities such as scoliosis; heart defects; and genital anomalies. Some affected males have undescended testes (cryptorchidism). PLS is caused by a duplication of genetic material on chromosome 4 at position q28. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
ref: Potocki-Lupski syndrome (PTLS) is a genetic disorder characterized by the presence of an extra copy of a tiny portion of chromosome 17 (duplication of 17p11.2). People with this duplication often have low muscle tone, poor feeding, and failure to thrive during infancy. They may also present with delayed development of motor and verbal milestones. In addition, many individuals display some behaviors commonly associated with autism spectrum disorders. While most cases of Potocki-Lupski syndrome occur sporadically, in rare cases, it may be inherited. Treatment involves physical, occupational, and speech therapy.
q: What is Potocki-Lupski syndrome?

answer: Mycosis fungoides is a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which is a cancer that affects the skin. This condition causes patches of abnormal skin cells to grow on the body's surface. These patches may be red and scaly, but they can also be white or yellowish. The patches usually occur on the arms, legs, torso, and face. In some cases, the patches spread to other parts of the body. Mycosis fungoides is often mistaken for eczema (a common skin disorder) because it has similar symptoms. However, unlike eczema, mycosis fungoides does not improve with treatment. Some people with mycosis fungoides develop another type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is a form of nonmelanoma skin cancer.
ref: Mycosis fungoides is the most common form of a type of blood cancer called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas occur when certain white blood cells, called T cells, become cancerous; these cancers characteristically affect the skin, causing different types of skin lesions. Although the skin is involved, the skin cells themselves are not cancerous. Mycosis fungoides usually occurs in adults over age 50, although affected children have been identified. Mycosis fungoides progresses slowly through several stages, although not all people with the condition progress through all stages. Most affected individuals initially develop skin lesions called patches, which are flat, scaly, pink or red areas on the skin that can be itchy. Cancerous T cells, which cause the formation of patches, are found in these lesions. The skin cells themselves are not cancerous; the skin problems result when cancerous T cells move from the blood into the skin. Patches are most commonly found on the lower abdomen, upper thighs, buttocks, and breasts. They can disappear and reappear or remain stable over time. In most affected individuals, patches progress to plaques, the next stage of mycosis fungoides. Plaques are raised lesions that are usually reddish, purplish, or brownish in color and itchy. Plaques commonly occur in the same body regions as patches. While some plaques arise from patches, others develop on their own, and an affected person can have both patches and plaques simultaneously. As with patches, cancerous T cells are found in plaques. Plaques can remain stable or can develop into tumors. Not everyone with patches or plaques develops tumors. The tumors in mycosis fungoides, which are composed of cancerous T cells, are raised nodules that are thicker and deeper than plaques. They can arise from patches or plaques or occur on their own. Mycosis fungoides was so named because the tumors can resemble mushrooms, a type of fungus. Common locations for tumor development include the upper thighs and groin, breasts, armpits, and the crook of the elbow. Open sores may develop on the tumors, often leading to infection. In any stage of mycosis fungoides, the cancerous T cells can spread to other organs, including the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and lungs, although this most commonly occurs in the tumor stage. In addition, affected individuals have an increased risk of developing another lymphoma or other type of cancer.
q: What is mycosis fungoides?

answer: Mutations in the GBE1 gene cause glycogen storage disease type VII. The GBE1 gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called glycogen branching enzyme. This enzyme is involved in the production of glycogen, which is stored in cells throughout the body and serves as a major energy reserve. Glycogen is made up of many smaller molecules called glucose units that are linked together in long chains. Glycogen branching enzyme adds extra branches to these chains by attaching one glucose unit to another at different points along the chain. Mutations in the GBE1 gene result in the production of an abnormal glycogen branching enzyme that cannot add branches to the glucose chains. As a result, glycogen is produced in a straight chain form instead of its usual branched structure. Straight-chain glycogen is less efficient than branched glycogen at storing large amounts of energy. It also breaks down more slowly when it is needed for energy production. A shortage of glycogen leads to low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) after meals and can lead to hypoglycemic coma. In addition, the lack of glycogen causes muscles to be weaker than normal (myopathy). These problems with muscle function contribute to the weakness and fatigue characteristic of glycogen storage disease type VII.
ref: Mutations in the PFKM gene cause GSDVII. This gene provides instructions for making one piece (the PFKM subunit) of an enzyme called phosphofructokinase, which plays a role in the breakdown of glycogen. The phosphofructokinase enzyme is made up of four subunits and is found in a variety of tissues. Different combinations of subunits are found in different tissues. In muscles used for movement (skeletal muscles), the phosphofructokinase enzyme is composed solely of PFKM subunits. In skeletal muscle, the cells' main source of energy is stored as glycogen. Glycogen can be broken down rapidly into the simple sugar glucose when energy is needed, for instance to maintain normal blood sugar levels between meals or for energy during exercise. Phosphofructokinase is involved in the sequence of events that breaks down glycogen to provide energy to muscle cells. PFKM gene mutations result in the production of PFKM subunits that have little or no function. As a result, no functional phosphofructokinase is formed in skeletal muscles, and glycogen cannot be completely broken down. Partially broken down glycogen then builds up in muscle cells. Muscles that do not have access to glycogen as an energy source become weakened and cramped following moderate strain, such as exercise, and in some cases, begin to break down. In other tissues, other subunits that make up the phosphofructokinase enzyme likely compensate for the lack of PFKM subunits, and the enzyme is able to retain some function. This compensation may help explain why other tissues are not affected by PFKM gene mutations. It is unclear why some individuals with GSDVII are affected with more severe forms of the disorder than others.
q: What are the genetic changes related to glycogen storage disease type VII?

answer: Your skin is the largest organ of your body. It protects you from germs and other harmful things. But it can also get infected. The most common skin infections are - Bacterial, such as impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, and boils - Fungal, such as athlete's foot, ringworm, and jock itch - Viral, such as warts and shingles Your doctor will diagnose an infection by looking at your symptoms and doing tests if needed. Treatment depends on what kind of infection you have. Some infections go away without treatment. Others may need medicine to treat them. You can help prevent skin infections by keeping your skin clean and dry. Avoid sharing towels and clothes that might carry germs. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

answer: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. The gene associated with this condition is located on the X chromosome, which is one of the two sex chromosomes. In males (who have only one X chromosome), one altered copy of the ABCD1 gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. In females (who have two X chromosomes), a mutation would have to occur in both copies of the gene to cause the disorder. Because it is unlikely that females will have two altered copies of this gene, males are affected by X-linked recessive disorders much more frequently than females. A characteristic of X-linked inheritance is that fathers cannot pass X-linked traits to their sons. Females with one altered copy of the ABCD1 gene usually do not experience any signs and symptoms of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. However, they can pass the altered gene to their children. If a female has one altered copy of the ABCD1 gene and one normal copy, she is called a carrier. Carriers of X-linked recessive disorders typically do not have any signs or symptoms of the disorder. When a carrier female has children, each child has a 50% chance to inherit the altered gene from her. Males who inherit the altered gene will develop the disorder; females who inherit the altered gene will also be carriers.
ref: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is inherited in an X-linked pattern. The signs and symptoms of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy tend to appear at a later age in females than in males. Affected women usually develop features of the adrenomyeloneuropathy type.

answer: Atopic dermatitis is considered to have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. In some cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from one affected parent.
ref: Allergic disorders tend to run in families; having a parent with atopic dermatitis, asthma, or hay fever raises the chances a person will develop atopic dermatitis. When associated with FLG gene mutations, atopic dermatitis follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, which means one copy of the altered FLG gene in each cell is sufficient to increase the risk of the disorder. Individuals with two altered copies of the gene are more likely to develop the disorder and can have more severe signs and symptoms than individuals with a single altered copy. When associated with other genetic factors, the inheritance pattern is unclear. People with changes in one of the genes associated with atopic dermatitis, including FLG, inherit an increased risk of this condition, not the condition itself. Not all people with this condition have a mutation in an associated gene, and not all people with a variation in an associated gene will develop the disorder.

ref: What are the signs and symptoms of Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency? Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency can have a significant effect on fetal development, which may become apparent during late pregnancy with poor fetal weight gain and decreasing levels of estriol in the urine of the mother during pregnancy. Delivery may be complicated, and babies may have low Apgar scores. A low birth weight is common. It has been suggested that there is a characteristic abnormal appearance associated with PDH deficiency, which may include a narrow head, prominent forehead (frontal bossing), wide nasal bridge, long philtrum and flared nostrils; however, these are not seen in all individuals and these features may occur with other disorders as well. Other abnormalities that have been reported include a simian crease, short neck, slight shortening of the limbs, flexion contractures (bent fingers), pes cavus (high arched foot), club foot, ventricular septal defect, and hydronephrosis. Individuals with PDH deficiency typically develop symptoms soon after birth. In general, there are two major types of onset: metabolic and neurological. The metabolic type presents as severe lactic acidosis (too much lactate in the bloodstream). This often does not respond to treatment, thus many of the individuals with this type of onset die during the newborn period (in very few cases, the lactic acidosis has been reported to respond to high doses of thiamine). Some individuals with severe lactic acidosis have also had severe hyperammonemia (high levels of ammonia in the blood). Individuals with the neurological type typically have hypotonia (poor muscle tone), poor feeding, and lethargy, and they later develop seizures. This type typically progresses to severe mental retardation, microcephaly (small head), blindness, and spasticity with secondary contractures (damage to muscles and tendons). However, long term survival is possible and several individuals with this type have reportedly reached their teens. Between these two extremes, there is a continuous range of intermediate forms. When the metabolic abnormalities (lactic acidosis and hyperammonemia) are less severe, the onset may be delayed until later in infancy, and these individuals may have intermittent episodes of lactic acidosis, which often is brought on by an illness and is associated with cerebellar ataxia (abnormal muscle movement). Some of the individuals with primarily neurological symptoms are said to have Leigh's disease. Although PDH deficiency occurs in males and females equally, the presentation of the disease differs between them. The metabolic type, especially the severe neonatal lactic acidosis, is much more common in males; the chronic, neurological form is much more common in females. answer: Is genetic testing available for lichen planus pigmentosus? Genetic testing is not currently available for lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP). In these cases, genetic testing can be used to identify individuals who are at increased risk of developing an autoimmune disorder. How is lichen planus pigmentosus diagnosed? A diagnosis of lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP) is usually made based on the presence of characteristic skin lesions. The following features are often present: - Lesions that are flat, pinkish-brown, and/or light brown in color - Lesions that are itchy - Lesions that occur on the arms, legs, trunk, and/or face - Lesions that do not cause pain or bleeding When possible, a biopsy of the affected skin should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

answer: The most common signs and symptoms of foodborne illness include - nausea - vomiting - diarrhea - fever - abdominal pain - headache - muscle aches - weakness - chills - loss of appetite - dehydration Symptoms usually begin 1 to 3 days after eating contaminated food, but they can appear as early as 1 hour or as late as 72 hours later. The length of time between eating contaminated food and developing symptoms varies depending on the type of contaminant. For example, symptoms from Salmonella infection may take up to 60 days to develop. Some people have no symptoms at all. Others may have only mild symptoms that go away without treatment. In some cases, however, symptoms can be severe enough to require hospitalization. People who are very young, elderly, pregnant women, or those with weakened immune systems are more likely to experience serious complications from foodborne illnesses.

answer: What causes Chiari malformation type 1? The exact cause of Chiari malformation type 1 is unknown, although it can be associated with other conditions such as spina bifida and myelomeningocele (a severe form of spina bifida). It may also occur sporadically in people who have no family history of the condition. In some cases, the condition appears to run in families; however, the genetic cause has not been identified.
ref: What causes Chiari malformation type 1? Primary or congenital Chiari malformations are caused by structural defects in the brain and spinal cord that occur during fetal development. The underlying cause of the structural defects are not completely understood, but may involve genetic mutations or lack of proper vitamins or nutrients in the maternal diet. Less frequently, Chiari malformation type 1 is acquired after birth. Causes of acquired Chiari malformation type 1 involve the excessive draining of spinal fluid from the lumbar or thoracic areas of the spine as a result of injury, exposure to harmful substances, or infection. answer: Is genetic testing available for eosinophilic enteropathy? Genetic testing is not currently available for eosinophilic enteropathy. The condition is thought to be caused by an immune system abnormality, and the underlying cause of this disorder is unknown.
ref: How is eosinophilic enteropathy diagnosed? Endoscopy and biopsy is the only way to confirm the diagnosis of eosinophilic enteropathy. During an endoscopy, a gastroenterologist looks at the gastrointestinal tract through an endoscope and takes multiple small samples (biopsies), which a pathologist reviews. A high number of eosinophils suggests the diagnosis of eosinophilic enteropathy. The pathologist will also look at the location of the eosinophils, changes in the tissue layers, and degranulation (spilling of the contents of the eosinophils). Eosinophils may be normally found in small numbers in all areas of the gastrointestinal tract except the esophagus. However, the number of eosinophils seen in individuals with eosinophilic enteropathy is much higher. Once the diagnosis of eosinophilic enteropathy is confirmed, food allergy testing is typically recommended to guide treatment. Tests for food allergies include skin prick testing, patch testing, and a Radioallergosorbent test (RAST).
q: How to diagnose Eosinophilic enteropathy?

answer: Epilepsy is a disorder of the brain that causes seizures. Seizures are sudden, uncontrolled electrical discharges in groups of nerve cells in your brain. They can cause - Convulsions - Loss of consciousness - Temporary confusion - Unusual behaviors - Sensory experiences such as seeing lights or hearing sounds There are many types of epilepsy and many different causes. Some people have only one seizure. Others have repeated seizures over time. The most common type of seizure is called tonic-clonic. It starts with stiffening of the body, then jerking movements. You may lose consciousness during this type of seizure. Other types of seizures include absence seizures, which make you stare blankly; myoclonic seizures, which cause sudden muscle spasms; and focal seizures, which affect only part of the brain. Treatment usually involves medicines to control seizures. Sometimes surgery is needed. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
ref: Epilepsy is a brain disorder that causes people to have recurring seizures. The seizures happen when clusters of nerve cells, or neurons, in the brain send out the wrong signals. People may have strange sensations and emotions or behave strangely. They may have violent muscle spasms or lose consciousness. Epilepsy has many possible causes, including illness, brain injury, and abnormal brain development. In many cases, the cause is unknown. Doctors use brain scans and other tests to diagnose epilepsy. It is important to start treatment right away. There is no cure for epilepsy, but medicines can control seizures for most people. When medicines are not working well, surgery or implanted devices such as vagus nerve stimulators may help. Special diets can help some children with epilepsy. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
q: What is Epilepsy?

Ovarian cancer starts in the ovaries. The ovaries are two egg-shaped organs in the pelvis on each side of the uterus. They make eggs and female hormones. The most common type of ovarian cancer is called epithelial ovarian cancer. This type of cancer begins in the cells that line the surface of the ovary. Ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers are diseases in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or peritoneum. The ovaries are a pair of organs in the female reproductive system. They are located in the pelvis, one on each side of the uterus (the hollow, pear-shaped organ where a fetus grows). Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond. The ovaries produce eggs and female hormones (chemicals that control the way certain cells or organs function). The fallopian tubes are a pair of long, slender tubes, one on each side of the uterus. Eggs pass from the ovaries, through the fallopian tubes, to the uterus. Cancer sometimes begins at the end of the fallopian tube near the ovary and spreads to the ovary. The peritoneum is the tissue that lines the abdominal wall and covers organs in the abdomen. Primary peritoneal cancer is cancer that forms in the peritoneum and has not spread there from another part of the body. Cancer sometimes begins in the peritoneum and spreads to the ovary. Ovarian epithelial cancer, fallopian tube cancer, and primary peritoneal cancer form in the same type of tissue. Studies of screening tests look at these cancers together. Since 2005, the number of deaths from ovarian cancer also decreased slightly in white and black women.

answer: What causes pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency (PDD)? PDD is caused by mutations in the E1 alpha, E1 beta, E2, and E3 genes. These genes provide instructions for making three different proteins that work together to form an enzyme called pyruvate dehydrogenase. This enzyme plays a critical role in converting sugars into energy. Mutations in any of these four genes can lead to a shortage (deficiency) of functional pyruvate dehydrogenase. A lack of this enzyme impairs the body's ability to convert sugars into energy, which leads to the signs and symptoms of PDD.
ref: What causes pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency? Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency is usually caused by a deficiency of one or more enzymes or cofactors (such as thiamine) that are needed for an important chemical reaction in the cells of the body. These enzymes or cofactors are part of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and normally convert (or aid in converting) a chemical called pyruvate to another chemical called acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA), which is one of two important chemicals the body needs to make citrate for the cells. Because pyruvate cannot be converted to acetyl-CoA, there is too much pyruvate in the cells, which then gets used to produce more lactic acid (which is toxic in large amounts) and alanine; there is also not enough citrate being made by the body. Citrate is the first step in another important group of chemical reactions called the citric acid cycle, which then cannot proceed. The body tries to make alternate pathways to produce more acetyl-CoA, but there is still not enough energy made in the body, especially in the central nervous system (CNS). The amount of energy that is deficient depends on the amount of the enzyme that is deficient. The condition is sometimes referred to as pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) deficiency because there is a "complex" of three enzymes normally used in the reaction; when any one or more of the enzymes needed for the above-described reaction are deficient, the condition results. The most common form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency is caused by mutations in the X-linked dominant E1 alpha gene; all other causes are thought to be due to mutations in recessive genes.
q: What causes Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency?

answer: Apraxia is a neurological disorder that affects the ability to plan and execute movements. It can affect any part of the body, but it most often affects the hands, feet, face, and mouth. People who have apraxia may be unable to perform tasks such as writing, eating, speaking, or walking. The condition usually results from damage to certain areas of the brain, including the cerebellum (the area at the back of the brain that coordinates movement), the basal ganglia (a group of structures deep within the brain that help control movement), and the cerebral cortex (the outer layer of the brain). Apraxia can also occur during strokes, head trauma, infections, tumors, and other conditions that cause brain injury. There are several types of apraxia: - Ideational apraxia involves an inability to plan and carry out complex actions. - Motor apraxia involves an inability to coordinate movements. - Constructional apraxia involves an inability to construct objects using available materials. - Verbal apraxia involves an inability to speak clearly. - Limb apraxia involves an inability to move one's arms and legs. Treatment depends on the type and severity of the condition.
ref: Apraxia (called "dyspraxia" if mild) is a neurological disorder characterized by loss of the ability to execute or carry out skilled movements and gestures, despite having the desire and the physical ability to perform them. Apraxia results from dysfunction of the cerebral hemispheres of the brain, especially the parietal lobe, and can arise from many diseases or damage to the brain. There are several kinds of apraxia, which may occur alone or together. The most common is buccofacial or orofacial apraxia, which causes the inability to carry out facial movements on command such as licking lips, whistling, coughing, or winking. Other types of apraxia include limb-kinetic apraxia (the inability to make fine, precise movements with an arm or leg), ideomotor apraxia (the inability to make the proper movement in response to a verbal command), ideational apraxia (the inability to coordinate activities with multiple, sequential movements, such as dressing, eating, and bathing), verbal apraxia (difficulty coordinating mouth and speech movements), constructional apraxia (the inability to copy, draw, or construct simple figures), and oculomotor apraxia (difficulty moving the eyes on command). Apraxia may be accompanied by a language disorder called aphasia. Corticobasal ganglionic degeneration is a disease that causes a variety of types of apraxia, especially in elderly adults.
q: What is Apraxia?

answer: Microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome (MELSD) is a condition that affects the development of many parts of the body, particularly the eyes and skin. People with this disorder have small, abnormally shaped eyes (microphthalmia). The eye abnormalities can be severe enough to cause blindness from birth or they may become apparent later in life as the affected person ages. In addition, people with MELSD often have other eye problems such as cataracts, glaucoma, and retinal detachment. Affected individuals also have distinctive facial features including a broad forehead; a flat bridge of bone between the nose and upper lip (philtrum); a long space between the nose and upper lip (a large philtrum); and a prominent chin. Other signs and symptoms of MELSD include short stature, an unusually small head size (microcephaly), and underdeveloped muscles (hypotonia). Individuals with MELSD typically have skin abnormalities called linear skin defects. These defects consist of thin lines of missing skin (atrophy) that run across the face and body. They usually occur along the midline of the body, which runs through the center of the body from the neck down to the hips. Linear skin defects can lead to scarring and abnormal growth of hair on the affected areas. Some people with MELSD have additional health problems, including heart defects, kidney malformations, and hearing loss.
ref: Microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome is a disorder that mainly affects females. In people with this condition, one or both eyes may be very small or poorly developed (microphthalmia). Affected individuals also typically have unusual linear skin markings on the head and neck. These markings follow the paths along which cells migrate as the skin develops before birth (lines of Blaschko). The skin defects generally improve over time and leave variable degrees of scarring. The signs and symptoms of microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome vary widely, even among affected individuals within the same family. In addition to the characteristic eye problems and skin markings, this condition can cause abnormalities in the brain, heart, and genitourinary system. A hole in the muscle that separates the abdomen from the chest cavity (the diaphragm), which is called a diaphragmatic hernia, may occur in people with this disorder. Affected individuals may also have short stature and fingernails and toenails that do not grow normally (nail dystrophy).
q: What is microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome?

answer: Hydrocephalus due to congenital stenosis of aqueduct of sylvius is not considered an inherited condition; however, it can occur as part of a genetic syndrome that has an inheritance pattern. For example, hydrocephalus due to congenital stenosis of aqueduct of sylvius may be associated with the following conditions: - Dandy-Walker malformation (which is caused by mutations in the ARX gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner) - Polycystic kidney disease type 1 (which is caused by mutations in the PKHD1 gene and is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner).
ref: Is hydrocephalus due to congenital stenosis of aqueduct of sylvius inherited? Hydrocephalus due to congenital stenosis of aqueduct of sylvius is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. A condition is X-linked if the responsible gene is located on the X chromosome. The X chromosome is one of the two sex chromosomes (the other sex chromosome is the Y chromosome). Females have two X chromosomes in each cell and males have an X chromosome and a Y chromosome in each cell. Although females have two X chromosomes, one of the X chromosomes in each cell is "turned off" and all of the genes on that chromosome are inactivated. Females who have a change (mutation) in a gene on one of their X chromosomes are called carriers of the related condition. Carrier females usually do not have symptoms of the condition because the X chromosome with the mutated gene is often turned off and they have another X chromosome with a working copy of the gene. Sometimes, the X chromosome with the working copy of the gene is turned off, which may cause symptoms of the condition. However, females with symptoms are usually much more mildly affected than males. A male has only one X chromosome, so if he inherits a mutation on the X chromosome, he will have signs and symptoms (be affected). Males with an X-linked recessive condition always pass the mutated gene to all of their daughters, who will be carriers. A male cannot pass an X-linked gene to his sons because males always pass their Y chromosome to male offspring. Female carriers of an X-linked recessive condition have a 25% chance with each pregnancy to have a carrier daughter like themselves, a 25% chance to have a non-carrier daughter, a 25% chance to have an affected son, and a 25% chance to have an unaffected son. This also means that each daughter of a carrier mother has a 50% chance of being a carrier, and each son has a 50% chance of having the condition.
q: Is Hydrocephalus due to congenital stenosis of aqueduct of sylvius inherited?

answer: Your doctor will use your medical and family histories, physical exam, and lab tests to diagnose diabetic kidney disease. Medical and Family Histories Your doctor may ask about - your symptoms - any other health problems you have - whether you smoke - your family history of diabetes and kidney disease Physical Exam During the physical exam, your doctor will listen to your heart and lungs with a stethoscope. He or she also will check your blood pressure and look for signs of swelling in your feet, ankles, legs, abdomen, face, or hands. Lab Tests A urine test can show if protein is leaking out of your kidneys into your urine. The test involves collecting a sample of your urine at home and sending it to a lab for analysis. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) is a common urine test used to measure how much albumin leaks out of your kidneys. UACR compares the amount of albumin in your urine to the amount of creatinine, a waste product that stays in your body. This comparison gives a more accurate picture of kidney function than just measuring the amount of albumin alone. If your UACR is 30 mg/g or higher, you have microalbuminuria. Microalbuminuria means that small amounts of albumin are leaking out of your kidneys into your urine. If your UACR is 300 mg/g or higher, you have macroalbuminuria. Macroalbuminuria means that larger amounts of albumin are leaking out of your kidneys into your urine. Blood tests can show if your kidneys are working well. They also can show if your blood sugar levels are too high. An estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) test measures how well your kidneys filter wastes from your blood. eGFR uses your age, sex, race, and other factors to estimate how well your kidneys are working. A GFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 means that your kidneys aren't working as well as they should. A GFR of less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 means that your kidneys aren't working well enough to keep up with the buildup of wastes in your body. To get an accurate eGFR result, you must have a blood test done on two separate days. You'll need to fast before having the blood test. A fasting period usually lasts eight hours. For more information, go to "What Are the Stages of Chronic Kidney Disease?"
ref: A health care provider diagnoses diabetic kidney disease based on - a medical and family history - a physical exam - urine tests - a blood test Medical and Family History Taking a medical and family history is one of the first things a health care provider may do to help diagnose diabetic kidney disease. He or she will ask about the symptoms and the patients diabetes history. Physical Exam After taking a medical and family history, a health care provider will perform a physical exam. During a physical exam, a health care provider usually - examines the patients body to check for changes in skin color - taps on specific areas of the patients body, checking for swelling of the feet, ankles, or lower legs Urine Tests Dipstick test for albumin. A dipstick test performed on a urine sample can detect the presence of albumin in the urine. A patient collects the urine sample in a special container in a health care providers office or a commercial facility. The office or facility tests the sample onsite or sends it to a lab for analysis. For the test, a nurse or technician places a strip of chemically treated paper, called a dipstick, into the urine. Patches on the dipstick change color when blood or protein is present in urine. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. A health care provider uses this measurement to estimate the amount of albumin passed into the urine over a 24-hour period. The patient collects a urine sample during an appointment with the health care provider. Creatinine is a waste product that is filtered in the kidneys and passed into the urine. A high urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio indicates that the kidneys are leaking large amounts of albumin into the urine. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio above 30 mg/g may be a sign of kidney disease. Blood Test A blood test involves having blood drawn at a health care providers office or a commercial facility and sending the sample to a lab for analysis. A health care provider may order a blood test to estimate how much blood the kidneys filter each minute, called the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). The results of the test indicate the following: - eGFR of 60 or above is in the normal range - eGFR below 60 may indicate kidney damage - eGFR of 15 or below may indicate kidney failure
q: How to diagnose Diabetic Kidney Disease?

answer: Mutations in the ALG6 gene cause ALG6-CDG. The ALG6 gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called alpha-L-galactosyltransferase 6, which is involved in the production (synthesis) of complex sugar molecules called glycans. Glycans attach to proteins and fats (lipids), modifying their structure and function. These modified molecules are known as glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. Glycans are attached to certain proteins and lipids on the surface of cells, where they play important roles in cell signaling, immune system function, and cell adhesion. Mutations in the ALG6 gene lead to the production of an abnormally short version of alpha-L-galactosyltransferase 6 that cannot perform its normal function. As a result, glycans are not properly attached to proteins and lipids. This abnormal modification impairs the function of many proteins and lipids, particularly those found on the surface of cells. It is unclear how these modifications contribute to the signs and symptoms of ALG6-CDG.
ref: ALG6-CDG is caused by mutations in the ALG6 gene. This gene provides instructions for making an enzyme that is involved in a process called glycosylation. Glycosylation is the process by which sugar molecules (monosaccharides) and complex chains of sugar molecules (oligosaccharides) are added to proteins and fats. Glycosylation modifies proteins and fats so they can perform a wider variety of functions. The enzyme produced from the ALG6 gene transfers a simple sugar called glucose to the growing oligosaccharide. Once the correct number of sugar molecules are linked together, the oligosaccharide is attached to a protein or fat. ALG6 gene mutations lead to the production of an abnormal enzyme with reduced or no activity. Without a properly functioning enzyme, glycosylation cannot proceed normally, and oligosaccharides are incomplete. As a result, glycosylation is reduced or absent. The wide variety of signs and symptoms in ALG6-CDG are likely due to impaired glycosylation of proteins and fats that are needed for normal function in many organs and tissues, including the brain, eyes, liver, and hormone-producing (endocrine) system.
q: What are the genetic changes related to ALG6-congenital disorder of glycosylation?

answer: Mevalonic aciduria is an inherited disorder that affects the body's ability to produce cholesterol and other fats (lipids). ref: Mevalonic aciduria is the severe form of mevalonate kinase deficiency, a condition characterized by recurrent episodes of fever that typically begin during infancy. Additional ongoing issues include developmental delay, progressive ataxia, progressive problems with vision, an unusually small, elongated head, and failure to thrive. answer: Sialidosis is an inherited disorder that affects many parts of the body, including the nervous system and organs such as the heart, liver, kidneys, and pancreas. The signs and symptoms of sialidosis vary among affected individuals, even within the same family. There are two types of sialidosis: type I and type II. Type I is characterized by progressive neurological problems beginning in childhood. Affected children may have developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and loss of speech (dysphasia). They also develop muscle weakness (myopathy) and atrophy (wasting), which can lead to difficulty walking. Other features include hearing loss, vision impairment, and a buildup of fluid in the abdomen (ascites). In addition, some people with this condition experience episodes of severe pain called gout attacks. Gout occurs when uric acid crystals build up in the joints and surrounding tissues. People with sialidosis type I typically survive into their teens or early 20s. Some individuals with sialidosis type I live longer than previously thought; however, they still face significant health challenges. Sialidosis type II has milder signs and symptoms than type I. It usually becomes apparent in adulthood. Most people with this form of the disorder do not have any neurological problems. Instead, they may develop kidney disease, liver disease, and/or diabetes mellitus. Rarely, people with sialidosis type II experience seizures and other neurological problems.
ref: Sialidosis is a severe inherited disorder that affects many organs and tissues, including the nervous system. This disorder is divided into two types, which are distinguished by the age at which symptoms appear and the severity of features. Sialidosis type I is the less severe form of this condition. People with this condition typically develop signs and symptoms of sialidosis in their teens or twenties. Characteristic features may include sudden involuntary muscle contractions (myoclonus), distinctive red spots (cherry-red macules) in the eyes, and sometimes additional neurological findings. Sialidosis type I is caused by mutations in the NEU1 gene. Individuals with sialidosis type I have mutations that result in some functional NEU1 enzyme. The condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It does not affect intelligence or life expectancy.
